# The Art of Wandering

I have been thinking lately about wandering—not the kind that requires a map, or a destination, or even a proper path, but the kind that happens when you put the map down and let the world take you by the elbow. It is an art, and like most arts, it has nearly disappeared from everyday life. We have become so good at moving from point A to point B, so efficient in our commutes and our schedules, that we have lost the ability to drift. We scroll, we swipe, we plan. We optimize. We measure our days in tasks completed, not in moments felt. But every now and then, if we are lucky, something breaks the rhythm—a sudden rain, a closed road, a forgotten appointment—and we find ourselves wandering again, not through space only, but through time and memory and attention. When that happens, I notice, the world looks different. It looks almost holy.

I remember a particular evening in late autumn. I was walking home through a neighborhood I knew well, the kind of neighborhood where every house has a lawn and every lawn has a sprinkler for the summer and a leaf pile for the fall. It was the hour before streetlights came on, when the sky turns the color of a bruise healing. I was not in a hurry, but I was not exactly present either. My mind was churning through the day’s small failures and the next day’s small tasks. Then something caught my eye: a crack in the sidewalk, spreading like a river delta. In that crack, a dandelion was growing. It was not a grand dandelion, not the kind you press into a book as a keepsake. It was stubborn, slightly yellowed, leaning as if it had been through a war. I stopped. I crouched. I looked at it for perhaps two minutes, which is a lifetime for a creature as restless as I usually am.

What struck me was not the dandelion itself, but the fact that I had passed this exact spot hundreds of times without ever seeing it. How many other things had I missed? How many small miracles had been performed in the margins of my vision while I stared at my phone or rehearsed conversations in my head? The dandelion was a kind of accusation. It asked me: what else are you not noticing? It was also an invitation. You could spend a whole life paying attention, it seemed to say, and still die unfinished.

That evening set me on a wandering course, not through any grand wilderness, but through the ordinary territories of my life. I began to walk without purpose. I began to look without expecting anything. I started to notice things I had been trained to ignore: the way light falls through a window at three in the afternoon, turning dust into gold; the particular weight of a doorknob when the house is empty; the sound of a refrigerator humming like a distant sea. These were not revelations in any dramatic sense. They were simply facts of existence, tiny and irreplaceable, waiting to be acknowledged. And the more I acknowledged them, the more the world seemed to thicken, to gain texture, to become something other than the flat backdrop of my ambitions.

There is a name for this, I learned later. The philosophers call it attention. William James wrote that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” He meant that reality is not a fixed thing, given to us whole, but a kind of allotment, parceled out by the focus of our minds. Two people can stand in the same room and live in entirely different worlds, depending on what they choose to see. The person who notices the dust motes in the sunbeam is not the same as the person who notices the crack in the wall, and neither is the same as the person who notices only the clock. Attention is not just a cognitive act. It is a moral act. It decides what counts. It decides what is real.

This is why the modern age is so troubling. We have more stimulation than any humans in history, yet we have less attention to give. Our devices are designed to capture us, to hold our gaze, to pull us toward the next notification with the precision of a fisherman’s hook. Every app is an engine of distraction. Every feed is a river of endless novelty. And in the middle of it, we sit, half-present, scrolling through other people’s lives while our own runs past us like a train we have forgotten to board. We are not wandering anymore. We are drifting, but not in the good way. We are drifting the way a plastic bag drifts across a parking lot—moved by every current, touching nothing, weighted by nothing.

The antidote, I think, is not to disconnect entirely. That is too simple, and too smug. The antidote is to reconnect with the local, the small, the particular. It is to walk down the same street a hundred times and try to see it as if for the first time. It is to sit with a cup of coffee and not reach for your phone, just to see what happens. It is to let your mind wander, not through a curated feed, but through the labyrinth of memory and desire and grief and wonder that you carry inside you. This kind of wandering is not passive. It is active. It requires courage. Because when you let your mind go where it wants to go, you will not always like the destination.

I tried this once, on a long bus ride through the countryside. I had no headphones. I had no book. I had only the window and the fields and the occasional farmhouse, and the strange, uncomfortable silence of my own skull. At first it was unbearable. I felt itchy, bored, almost panicked. My hand kept twitching toward my pocket. But I forced myself to stay. I watched the fences go by. I watched the cows lift their heads, one by one, as the bus roared past. I thought about a summer I spent at my grandmother’s house when I was nine years old, and how the hedges smelled of nettles and rain, and how she would kneel in her garden for hours, weeding, and I would kneel beside her, thinking she was moving too slowly. She told me once: “You have to know a plant before you can pull it up.” I thought she meant get close enough to see its leaves, but now I understand she meant something deeper. You have to know why it is there. You have to know what it is doing, what it is becoming, what it is holding in its roots. Only then can you decide if it belongs.

That bus ride became a kind of pilgrimage. Not because I was going anywhere sacred, but because I was returning to myself. Memory does that. It ambushes you. A smell, a sound, a particular quality of light, and suddenly you are not an adult on a bus; you are a child in a garden, and the world is enormous and tender and full of small things that matter. We spend so much of our lives trying to escape our memories, to outrun them, to curate them into something neat and presentable. But the memories that truly shape us are not neat. They are ragged. They are full of contradictions. They are like the dandelion in the crack, refusing to be pulled up, insisting on their place in the concrete.

I think that is why I have come to love the poetry of ordinary objects. A kitchen table, for instance. I once sat at a kitchen table in a house that was being emptied for an estate sale. The owners had died—an old couple, no children—and the furniture was being sold to strangers. I was there because I knew the family, and I wanted to pay my respects, but also because I was curious. What remains of a life after it leaves? I walked through the rooms and saw the artifacts: a clock that had stopped, a stack of newspapers from a decade ago, a pair of glasses resting on a windowsill. In the kitchen, there was a table with a worn surface, scarred by years of knives and coffee cups and elbows. I put my hand on it, and I felt something—not literally, but I felt it nonetheless: the weight of all those meals, all those conversations, all those mornings when the light came through the window and fell across the same scarred wood. The table was not valuable. But it was full. It was full of time.

There is a word for this kind of fullness. The Greeks called it kairos—the unstretched moment, the time that is experienced rather than measured. We live mostly in chronos, the time of clocks and calendars, the time that ticks relentlessly forward. But kairos is the time of the dandelion in the crack. It is the time of the old kitchen table. It is the time you enter when you forget to check your phone, when you lose yourself in a conversation or a walk or a task that asks for every part of you. Kairos is not a luxury. It is a necessity. Without it, life becomes a series of tasks, a checklist, a countdown. With it, life becomes something else: a story, a song, a prayer.

I do not want to be romantic about this. Wandering is not always pleasant. Sometimes it leads you into dark places—into grief, into regret, into the small hard rooms of your own disappointments. I have sat by the window on many nights, watching the rain, and felt the full weight of all the things I have failed to do and all the people I have failed to be. But even that, I think, is part of the art. To be fully human is to be able to hold the darkness and the light in the same hand. To wander is to accept that you will not always have a map, and that sometimes the best you can do is to keep moving, step by step, paying attention as you go.

There is a story I like about the Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō. He was traveling through the northern provinces of Japan, on foot, writing haiku as he went. He did not have a destination in the modern sense. He had a direction, and a longing, and an enormous capacity for wonder. When he saw a horse grazing in a field, he wrote a poem. When he saw a snake crossing a road, he wrote a poem. When he saw a temple gate overgrown with moss, he wrote a poem. He was not trying to capture anything. He was letting the world in, and the world filled him until he had to let it out again in words. That is what I want my life to be. Not a series of achievements, but a series of encounters. Not a résumé, but a notebook. Not a destination, but a path—wandering, winding, always showing me something new.

I have started taking walks again. Not the brisk, purposeful walks of exercise, but the slow, aimless walks of a child. I go out without a plan. I turn left or right depending on which tree looks interesting. I stop to watch a crow wrestle with a piece of bread. I sit on a bench and watch the clouds rearrange themselves. I have learned the names of a few wildflowers: queen anne’s lace, chicory, goldenrod. I have learned to identify the call of a blue jay and the rustle of a squirrel in the leaves. These are small things, I know. But they are not nothing. They are the opposite of nothing. They are the threads out of which a life is woven, and I had forgotten how much thread I was letting slip through my fingers.

The strange thing is that this wandering has made me more productive, not less. By giving myself permission to be idle, I have given my mind permission to work on its own schedules. Ideas arrive when I am not looking for them. Solutions come when I am not forcing them. It is as if the mind is a river, and I had been trying to dam it with effort; when I stopped, when I let it flow, it found its own way to the sea. I wonder how many breakthroughs, personal and collective, are lost to us because we are too busy to wander. I wonder how many inventions, how many poems, how many acts of kindness are waiting in the margins of our attention, in the moments we dismiss as wasted.

There is a phrase in the Christian tradition: “pray without ceasing.” I have never been able to take that literally, but I think I understand it now. To pray without ceasing is to live in a state of constant openness to the world. It is to see the divine in the ordinary, the sacred in the mundane. It is to treat every encounter, every object, every breath as an occasion for gratitude. And gratitude, I think, is the root of everything. When I crouched on the sidewalk and looked at that dandelion, I felt a flood of gratitude—not for the dandelion itself, exactly, but for the fact that I had been given the chance to see it. For the fact that the world is so endlessly, abundantly full of things worth noticing. For the fact that I am alive, in this moment, in this body, on this earth, with all its cracks and all its flowers.

We live in a time that tells us to hurry. To do more, to be more, to consume more. But I have come to believe that the most radical act we can perform is to slow down. To stop. To look. To wander. To let the moment unfold without forcing it to be something else. The dandelion did not ask for my attention. It simply grew, in the crack, in the concrete, in the light of the dying day. And when I gave it my attention, it gave me something in return. It gave me a reminder: that life is not in the distance, over the hill, in the future we are always rushing toward. It is here. It is now. It is in the crack. It is in the flower. It is in the hand that reaches down to touch a leaf, and the breath that carries the faint scent of rain, and the heart that, for one brief moment, is entirely present.

So this is my small gospel, if you can call it that: wander more. Not physically, necessarily. Mentally. Emotionally. Spiritually. Let your thoughts go where they want, even if they are afraid. Look at the things you have always taken for granted as if you are seeing them for the first time. Sit with the uncomfortable silences. Wait for the world to speak to you, and when it does, listen. You will not get a second chance at this moment. This moment, right now, is already slipping away. The only way to hold it is to notice it. The only way to keep it is to let it go, and in the letting go, to be fully there.

I have not reached the end of my wandering. I do not expect to. The path unfolds as I walk, and it will continue to unfold long after I am gone. But I am learning, slowly, to trust it. To trust the cracks in the sidewalk. To trust the wildflowers and the weeds. To trust the old kitchen tables and the empty houses and the rain on the window. To trust that if I pay attention, the world will show me what I need to see. And perhaps, in some small way, that is enough. Perhaps that is everything. The art of wandering is the art of being alive. And it is never too late to begin.
